title: How To Give A Reminder That Improves Behavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/09/29/how-to-give-a-reminder-that-improves-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Following up on his earlier warning against post-misbehavior reminders, Linsin describes a proactive reminder technique used before misbehavior can occur. The seven-step process involves signaling for attention, using the phrase 'in a moment' to freeze students mentally, creating a vivid verbal visualization of the expected behavior using 'you' language, employing a clear 'go' signal, breaking the reminder into simple steps, and finally challenging students to confirm they understand before releasing them. After giving the go signal, he instructs teachers to simply watch without further guiding, encouraging, or correcting. The strategy aims to give students total clarity and ownership over expectations so they can perform routines with confidence and independence.
points: A proactive reminder given before releasing students to a task differs fundamentally from a reactive, post-misbehavior reminder.
The phrase 'in a moment' mentally freezes students so they focus fully before moving, rather than half-listening while already acting.
Verbal visualization using 'you' language ('you're going to...') creates a mental movie that helps students perform the task successfully.
A clear 'go' signal and a final challenge question ('is there anyone who doesn't know exactly what to do?') ensure full understanding before release.
After the go signal, teachers should simply watch without guiding, encouraging, or correcting, letting students perform independently.
quotes: Your students must prove to you they’re able to perform routines and procedures without your guidance before putting them into day-to-day practice.
Stand in one place and signal for your students’ attention—then wait a beat or two to ensure that every eye is on you and every ear is tuned to your same frequency.
Instead of saying, “remember to do this or do that,” what you’re going to do is preview for your students, in the form of a visualization, or movie in their mind, exactly what you expect from them.
The phrase, “when I say go” is another effective technique that helps students relax and focus on listening.
This final questioning technique adds a final shovelful of responsibility. And because you left nothing to chance, you can give your ‘go’ signal knowing your students will do exactly what you want.
Provide them the tools they need to succeed . . . And then fade into the background and let them shine.
